Aaron Schwartz | Afp | Getty Images The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system managed by contractor L3Harris Technologies , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded by lingering disruptions. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy. The upgrades at "at least" one remote location were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Duffy said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, the secretary said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. headlines.article_text: Italy fines Meta $887 million over Android users' data access Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A worker stands inside the Meta Lab in Los Angeles, California, May 20, 2026. Daniel Cole | Reuters Italy's data protection agency said on Saturday it had fined Meta Platforms 805 million euros ($887 million) after finding the company had accessed Android users' photographs and videos without obtaining their consent or informing them. Meta had access to Android users' photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that suggested content from users' personal galleries that they could post, the authority said in a statement Meta has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately, it said. A Meta spokesperson said the company would appeal, strongly disagreeing with the authority's decision and calling the fine "disproportionate." "This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook.
